by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.intervention: Cold showers, cold-water immersion or winter swimming
question.comparison: Warm showers or no cold exposure
question.outcome: Sickness absence, days of illness or infections

decisions.reason: Reviews randomised trials of cold showers or immersion in healthy adults and reports sickness absence (29% reduction with cold showers) in its narrative synthesis.

question.population: Adults suddenly immersed in cold water, healthy or winter swimmers
question.outcome: Heart rate, blood pressure, heart rhythm, breathing, or how these change with repeated immersion

decisions.reason: Reviews cold-water immersion and heart rate variability, but only in athletes recovering after exercise, not sudden immersion in healthy adults.
Meta-analysis of repeated cold-water immersion in people, pooling heart rate and breathing changes as the cold shock response habituates.
Healthy adults with heart rate, blood pressure and HRV outcomes, but cold-water immersion is pooled with cryostimulation and not clearly analysed alone.
Reviews L-citrulline supplements for blood pressure in cold environments, not the effects of cold-water immersion.

question.population: Adults, healthy or with low mood
question.intervention: Cold showers, cold-water immersion or winter swimming
question.comparison: No cold exposure, or warm water
question.outcome: Mood, stress, wellbeing, depression, anxiety or sleep

decisions.reason: Pools randomised trials of cold showers or cold-water immersion in healthy adults, measuring sleep, stress, mood, wellbeing, depression and anxiety.
Pools studies, including controlled ones, of cold showers, immersion or winter swimming in adults, measuring mood, stress, depression, anxiety, wellbeing and sleep.
This is only a protocol for a planned review, so it reports no pooled or reviewed results yet, although its question matches.
It covers whole-body cryotherapy (cold air), not cold water, used as an add-on treatment in people with mental health problems; outcomes include depression.
This is about cold stress in maize leaves, not people.
It covers whole-body cryotherapy (cold air) and hyperbaric oxygen for depression, not cold-water exposure, in patients rather than healthy adults or people with low mood.
This is about cold acclimation in plant cell membranes, not human cold exposure or mood.

question.intervention: Regular cold-water immersion after training sessions
question.comparison: The same training without cold water
question.outcome: Gains in muscle size or strength

decisions.reason: Compares cryotherapy with photobiomodulation for short-term muscle recovery, not regular cold water versus none for strength or size gains.
Looks at one cold-water bath and short-term strength recovery, not regular use alongside strength training for long-term gains.
Umbrella review that includes how regular post-exercise cold water affects resistance training adaptations, reporting on both strength and muscle growth.
Looks at one cold-water bath and recovery from muscle damage, not regular use during strength training for strength or size gains.
Compares water and cold therapies for short-term recovery from muscle damage, not training-induced gains in muscle size or strength.
Resistance-training group matches, but it compares cold-water protocols for short-term recovery after sessions, not long-term strength or size gains.
Pools controlled studies of regular cold water during resistance training versus none, with training-induced strength changes analysed separately.
Meta-analysis of cold water after resistance training sessions versus control on strength gains.
Reviews the short-term effects of cryotherapy on athletes' strength, flexibility and control, not regular use alongside strength training for gains.

question.intervention: Repeated cold exposure (cold air, cold water or winter swimming)
question.outcome: Brown fat activity, energy expenditure, insulin sensitivity or blood sugar

decisions.reason: Looks at habitual cold and brown fat activity, but only in Arctic residents, mostly from observational studies with no clear no-cold comparison group.
Pools trials of cold exposure versus thermoneutral conditions in healthy adults, with glucose and insulin as outcomes.
Systematically reviews trials in adults that include cold exposure as one intervention, with energy expenditure and brown fat activation as outcomes.
Looks at seasonal air temperature and FT3 thyroid hormone levels, not deliberate repeated cold exposure or the named outcomes.
Pools trials of cold versus room temperature on energy expenditure and brown fat, but the exposure is acute rather than repeated.
Reviews exercise training and UCP1 in brown fat in animals, not cold exposure in adults.
Reviews dietary compounds such as capsinoids and catechins for activating brown fat, not cold exposure.

question.population: Adults after hard or unaccustomed exercise, mostly young and active
question.intervention: Cold-water immersion (or other cooling) after exercise
question.outcome: Muscle soreness, or recovery of strength and performance

decisions.reason: Trials in athletes or active people compared cold-water immersion with control and measured soreness and performance recovery.
Cold-water immersion after exercise in athletes, but recovery was measured only by heart rate variability, not soreness or performance.
Cryotherapy after exercise was compared with light therapy, not with rest or no cooling.
Looked at the body's physiological response to brief cold immersion, mostly in resting people, not at soreness or performance after exercise.
Whole-body cryotherapy, a form of cooling, was compared with rest or control for muscle soreness in young active adults after exercise.
Pooled 52 studies of single-session cold-water immersion after exercise for muscle soreness (DOMS) and muscle damage markers.
Compared cold-water immersion with body cryotherapy head to head; no comparison with rest or no cooling.
Cold-water immersion vs control after matches in trained soccer players, measuring strength, jump, sprint and soreness.
Umbrella review of reviews on cold-water immersion after exercise vs comparators, covering soreness and performance outcomes.
Network meta-analysis of cold-water immersion and other cryotherapy vs control after exercise, covering soreness and jump performance.
A single randomised crossover trial, not a systematic review.
RCTs of a single cold-water immersion vs passive recovery after exercise, covering strength, power and soreness.
Pooled cold-water immersion alone after exercise, analysed separately from combined therapy, for soreness and jump performance.
Network meta-analysis of cold-water immersion doses vs control after muscle-damaging exercise, for soreness and jump performance.
Umbrella review of meta-analyses on cold-water immersion vs passive rest after exercise, for performance and soreness.
RCTs of cold-water immersion vs seated passive rest after exercise, measuring soreness, strength and jump.
Network meta-analysis of cold-water immersion and cryotherapy after muscle-damaging exercise, for soreness and jump ability.
Meta-analysis of cold-water immersion after hard exercise, for soreness, perceived effort and jump performance.
Network meta-analysis of cold and heat therapies, including passive recovery, for soreness after exercise.
RCTs of cold-water immersion vs control for muscle soreness after exercise in athletes and non-athletes.
Meta-analysis of cold-water immersion after exercise, measuring recovery of strength, jump, sprint and endurance performance plus muscle soreness.
Physically active adults and the right outcomes, but cold-water immersion is compared with other recovery methods, not with rest or no cooling.
Pools trials of cold therapy, with cold-water immersion analysed on its own, given within 1 h after exercise for muscle soreness (DOMS).
Cold-water immersion compared with passive recovery after hard exercise in active people, measuring performance and muscle soreness.
Cooling after muscle-damaging exercise, but it compares whole-body with partial-body cryotherapy instead of with rest or no cooling.
Cold-water immersion after team sport, pooled for jump, sprint, fatigue and muscle soreness outcomes in athletes.
Cooling (mainly cold-water immersion) compared with passive non-cooling recovery after exhausting exercise, with muscle soreness pooled.
Randomised trials of cold-water immersion compared with passive recovery after exercise, measuring muscle soreness.
Cold applications for recovery and muscle soreness, but the population is adolescent athletes, not adults.
No abstract; the title says it is a meta-analysis of cold-water immersion for recovery from strenuous exercise.
No abstract; the title says it is a meta-analysis of cold-water immersion to improve recovery after exercise.
Cold-water immersion compared with control, but the outcome is core body temperature, not muscle soreness or performance recovery.
Randomised trials of cooling after exercise in trained athletes, measuring recovery of sprint, endurance, jump and strength performance.
